name: TCP Abnormality Detection — Scan Types, RST Injection & Hijacking
description: TCP scan detection via flag analysis: SYN scans (half-open), NULL scans (no flags), ACK scans (firewall mapping), FIN scans, and Xmas scans (all flags). RST injection terminates connections by spoofing src IP + RST flag. TCP hijacking uses sequence number prediction + ARP poisoning to inject into active sessions. All detectable via Wireshark TCP flag filters and MAC address cross-referencing.
source: CDSA Module 08: Intermediate Network Traffic Analysis
notes:
=== TCP FLAGS REFERENCE ===
URG = Urgent data (rarely used legitimately)
ACK = Acknowledgement (almost always set after handshake)
PSH = Push (deliver data to app immediately)
RST = Reset (abort connection)
SYN = Synchronize (initiate connection)
FIN = Finish (graceful close)
ECN = Explicit Congestion Notification

=== TCP 3-WAY HANDSHAKE (NORMAL) ===
  Client → Server: SYN
  Server → Client: SYN-ACK
  Client → Server: ACK
  → Then data transfer with PSH+ACK
  → Close: FIN-ACK → FIN-ACK → ACK

Anomalies to watch:
  1. Too many flags of one kind (scanning)
  2. Unusual flag combinations (NULL, Xmas)
  3. One source → many ports or many hosts
  4. SYN floods from random sources

=== SCAN TYPE DETECTION ===

[SYN SCAN] — Most common Nmap scan
Behavior:
  → Attacker sends SYN; open port responds SYN-ACK; attacker sends RST
  → Closed port responds RST directly
  → IOC: many SYN packets from one IP to many ports
Filter:
  tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0    → SYN packets only
  → Follow with: ip.src == <SCANNER_IP>
  → Also watch for: one host generating many RST to close scanner's half-open

[NULL SCAN] — No flags set
Behavior:
  → Open port: no response
  → Closed port: RST response
  → IOC: TCP packets with no flags → RST replies from closed ports
Filter:
  tcp.flags == 0      → packets with zero flags (NULL scan)

[ACK SCAN] — Maps firewall rules (not service detection)
Behavior:
  → Both open AND closed ports respond with RST
  → Purpose: determine if port is filtered (no response = firewall) vs unfiltered (RST)
  → IOC: many ACK packets from one source → RST replies back
Filter:
  tcp.flags.ack == 1 && tcp.flags.syn == 0 && tcp.flags.fin == 0
  → Many ACKs from same source to many ports

[FIN SCAN] — Stealthy, bypass some firewalls
Behavior:
  → Open port: no response
  → Closed port: RST response
  → IOC: FIN packets without SYN/ACK preceding them
Filter:
  tcp.flags.fin == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0    → FIN-only packets

[XMAS SCAN] — All flags set (FIN+PSH+URG)
Behavior:
  → Open port: no response
  → Closed port: RST response
  → IOC: impossible flag combination (FIN+PSH+URG set simultaneously)
Filter:
  tcp.flags.fin == 1 && tcp.flags.push == 1 && tcp.flags.urg == 1
  → Very obvious — legitimate traffic never uses all three together

=== GENERAL SCAN DETECTION APPROACH ===
  1. Filter for scan flag pattern (see above per scan type)
  2. Apply: ip.src == <SUSPECTED_SCANNER>
  3. Check Statistics → Conversations → TCP tab
     → One host talking to many ports = scan
  4. Look for RST flood from victim to scanner (many closed ports)
  5. Correlate with IDS alerts or server logs

=== TCP RST INJECTION (CONNECTION TERMINATION ATTACK) ===
How it works:
  1. Attacker spoofs source IP of victim machine
  2. Sends TCP RST to destination with correct port
  3. Destination terminates connection thinking victim requested it
Result: DoS on any active TCP connection

Detection steps:
  1. Filter: tcp.flags.rst == 1 → look for RST flood to one port
  2. Open packet → check Ethernet → Source MAC
  3. Cross-reference: does src IP's registered MAC match what's actually sending?
  4. Mismatch = spoofed RST injection
Filter:
  tcp.flags.rst == 1 && ip.src == <VICTIM_IP>
  → Then check eth.src in Packet Details — if MAC doesn't match known host = attack

IOC: excessive RST packets to one port, MAC in ethernet header doesn't match ARP table entry for that IP

=== TCP CONNECTION HIJACKING ===
How it works:
  1. Attacker monitors active TCP session
  2. Predicts next sequence number (seq prediction or sniffing)
  3. Spoofs victim's src IP, injects packet in correct order
  4. Blocks ACKs from reaching victim (often via ARP poisoning)
Result: attacker takes over existing authenticated session

Detection signs:
  → TCP retransmissions in stream (victim not getting ACKs)
  → Out-of-order packets from one host
  → PSH+ACK packets arriving from unexpected MAC for victim's IP
  → Often combined with ARP poisoning (check for duplicate-address-detected)
Filter:
  tcp.analysis.retransmission    → find retransmissions
  tcp.analysis.out_of_order      → find out-of-order segments

Note: TCP hijacking commonly targets Telnet (port 23) since it's cleartext and easy to inject into.
